books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835

stimulus.text:
Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), on the peoples of the United States:

“Three races naturally distinct, and I might almost say hostile to each other, are discoverable among them at the first glance. ... fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart.”

“As soon as it is admitted that the whites and the emancipated blacks are placed upon the same territory in the situation of two alien communities, it will readily be understood that there are but two alternatives for the future; the negroes and the whites must either wholly part or wholly mingle.”

“I do not imagine that the white and black races will ever live in any country upon an equal footing.”

Background: Tocqueville, a French visitor, traveled in the United States in 1831–1832 and published Democracy in America in 1835.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (Reeve translation, 1835), public domain, as printed on Wikisource.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (1835), public domain
stem: A historian using this passage should be most careful about which of the following?

options.text: Tocqueville wrote in French, so no American read his book
options.misconception: The book was translated into English and widely read in America.

options.text: Tocqueville never visited the United States at all
options.misconception: Tocqueville toured the United States in 1831 and 1832.

options.text: Tocqueville wrote in 1835, before Texas and the Mexican War
Tocqueville supported slavery and wanted it to spread
options.misconception: Nothing in the passage defends slavery. Tocqueville writes about it as a danger to the Union, not as a good.

rationales.A: The book was translated and read in America. Writing first in French did not keep Americans from reading it.
rationales.B: The background note says he traveled in the United States in 1831 and 1832. He saw the country himself.
rationales.C: A witness from 1835 cannot describe the 1840s. His warning predates Texas and the Mexican War, so use it for its own time.
rationales.D: Nothing in the passage defends slavery. Tocqueville writes about it as a danger to the Union, not as a good.
rationales.general:
1. Ask when the witness wrote. Tocqueville published in 1835, after a tour in 1831 and 1832.
2. Ask what came later. Texas joined the Union in 1845, and the Mexican War followed in 1846.
3. Name the limit. His warning is strong evidence about 1835, and only a forecast about the 1840s.
Background: Tocqueville was a French aristocrat writing for French readers, not an American voter.
Remember: always check a source's date against the events you want it to explain.
